evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 說文釋形 / 字樣說明 / 釋義
evidence.text: The entry transcribes the Shuowen analysis of 汽 as “water dried up,” alternatively “tears falling,” formed 从水，气聲. It also quotes the Shijing phrase 汽可小康 and cites Jiyun for “water vapor.” Its editorial note says modern 汽 specializes in compounds such as water vapor and gasoline, while the older senses are now carried by 汔. The entry does not date that shift.
evidence.title: 汽 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The entry likewise analyzes 汽 as 从水、气聲 and associates that analysis with “water dried up”; it reports the vapor sense via Jiyun as 汽，水氣也. This is a dictionary report of older sources, not an independently dated occurrence of the vapor sense.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 汽

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The related 汔 entry repeats the Shuowen water-dried gloss and cites the Shijing line 民亦勞止，汔可小康 with the sense “nearly.” It also cites Bao Puzi for a use meaning “make dry.” This shows meanings recorded under 汔 but does not establish a dated process by which meanings moved from 汽 to 汔.
evidence.title: 汔 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.field: 同聲符字 / 上古漢語
evidence.text: Lists Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003) Old Chinese *kʰɯds for 汽 and *kʰɯds among the readings for 气, consistent with a phonetic relationship in the compound. This is a secondary account; its separate ideogrammic “water + air” alternative is not supported by the Shuowen graphic analysis recorded in the inspected primary dictionary.
evidence.title: 汽 - 维基词典

search_audit.query: 汽 《集韻》水氣也 汽可小康 詩經 民亦勞止 汔
search_audit.outcome: MOE entries confirm the Shijing wording and dictionary-reported vapor sense. No date for the first vapor use or a semantic bridge was established.

gaps: No directly inspected archaeological oracle-bone, bronze, or manuscript form of 汽 was found. The MOE page reproduces the Shuowen small-seal form as an image, but its pixels were not inspected; earlier graphic development and possible corruption remain unresolved.

The primary dictionary accounts support the phono-semantic analysis 水 + 气聲. An interpretation of 气 as a semantic air element is only a secondary proposal in the inspected material; evidence does not establish it as an additional original intent.

The Shijing phrase is reproduced in the Shuowen account, and the MOE 汔 entry cites the Shijing use 汔 “nearly.” The inspected sources do not establish that the phrase was originally written with the same graph in its earliest witness, nor do they date that orthographic history.

The vapor sense is reported through Jiyun, but no date for the cited entry or earliest attestation was established. The semantic relationship between ‘water dried up’/‘tears falling’ and ‘water vapor’ remains undocumented.
The dictionary says 汔 now carries the older senses, but no dated sequence or scribal explanation for the reassignment was found. No evidence of graphic corruption was established.

No exact Xiaoxuetang 汽 record or reusable image URL was obtained, and no verified Commons description page for a 汽 historical glyph was established; consequently no historical glyph images are proposed.

The provided local primary-reading metadata gives 汽 Mandarin qì but no 气 row. Character-specific Unicode Unihan pages were not inspected in this run, so no official Unihan reading citation is asserted. Local row provenance cannot substitute for an external click-through record.
No repository row was emitted as external evidence. No tracked extract recommendation is made; consulted dictionary content is paraphrased and linked character by character.

limitations.text: No usable, exact historical glyph image URL with inspected character-specific identity and provenance was established. Xiaoxuetang’s query interface and CC0 notice were inspected, but no 汽-specific record could be retrieved; Commons search likewise did not yield an inspected exact description page. The Shuowen small-seal form is recorded by the MOE dictionary, but its glyph pixels were not inspected and no image URL is proposed.
